before: Forord + Stemning + Lovtale over Abraham + Foreløbig Expectoration + 3 Problemata + Epilog (8 kapitler)
after: Forord, fire variationer over Abraham, en lovtale, en indledning, tre filosofiske problemer og en epilog

before: Ikke blot i handelens, men også i idéernes verden foranstalter vor tid ein wirklicher Ausverkauf. Alt fås for en sådan spotpris, at det bliver et spørgsmål, om der til sidst er nogen, der vil byde. Enhver spekulativ marqueur, der samvittighedsfuldt pointerer den nyere filosofis betydningsfulde gang, enhver privatdocent, repetent, student, enhver udflytter og indsidder i filosofien bliver ikke stående ved at tvivle om alt, men går videre. Måske ville det være utidigt og ubetimeligt at spørge dem, hvor de dog egentlig kommer hen, men høfligt og beskedent er det vel at anse det for afgjort, at de har tvivlet om alt, da det jo ellers var en besynderlig tale, at de gik videre.
after:
Dialektisk lyrik af Johannes de silentio.

_Was Tarquinius Superbus in seinem Garten mit den Mohnköpfen sprach, verstand der Sohn, aber nicht der Bote._ — Hamann
[Det, Tarquinius Superbus sagde med valmuehovederne i sin have, forstod sønnen, men ikke budbringeren.]

I vores tid holder man udsalg, og det gælder også idéerne: _ein wirklicher Ausverkauf_, et rigtigt ophørsudsalg. Alt er så billigt, at man til sidst må spørge, om nogen overhovedet vil byde. Enhver filosofisk billardmarkør, der samvittighedsfuldt tæller point, mens den nyere filosofi gør sine store fremskridt, enhver privatdocent, hjælpelærer og student, enhver nybygger og lejer på filosofiens jord nøjes ikke med at tvivle på alt, men går videre. Det ville måske være både taktløst og utidigt at spørge, hvor de egentlig kommer hen. Så er det vel høfligt og beskedent at gå ud fra, at de har tvivlet på alt. Ellers ville det jo lyde underligt, at de gik videre. Så langt er de altså alle nået, og sikkert så let, at ingen synes, det er nødvendigt at sige et ord om hvordan. Selv den, der ængsteligt og bekymret søgte den mindste oplysning, fandt intet, intet lille vink, ikke så meget som en leveregel for den, der står over for så vældig en opgave. »Men Descartes gjorde det jo?« Descartes var en beskeden, hæderlig tænker, der fortjener vores respekt. Man kan næppe læse hans skrifter uden at blive dybt berørt. Han gjorde, hvad han sagde, og sagde, hvad han gjorde. Ak! Ak! Ak! Hvor er det sjældent i vores tid!

before:
Frygt og Bæven kredser om en enkelt fortælling fra Første Mosebog, kapitel 22: Gud befaler Abraham at tage sin søn Isak med op på Morija-bjerget og dræbe ham som brændoffer, og Abraham adlyder. Han sadler sit æsel ved daggry, vandrer tre dage i tavshed, bygger alteret, binder sin søn og løfter kniven. Englen standser hans hånd. Bogen spørger, hvordan det er muligt at kalde denne mand troens fader frem for en morder, og hvilken slags tro der ville kræves for at være ham. Kierkegaard genfortæller Morija-historien på fire forskellige måder i de indledende sider. Han sammenligner Abraham med Agamemnon i Aulis, med den græske tragedies tragiske helt, med Maria ved bebudelsen, med havmanden fra dansk folkesagn. Omkring fortællingen bygger han et systematisk argument i tre problemata: om der findes en teleologisk suspension af det etiske, om der findes en absolut pligt mod Gud, og om Abrahams tavshed over for Sara og Isak var etisk forsvarlig.

Kierkegaard udgav bogen i København i oktober 1843, som tredivearig, under pseudonymet Johannes de Silentio — samme uge, som han udgav Gjentagelsen. Han havde hævet sin forlovelse med Regine Olsen to år tidligere og kunne ikke holde op med at skrive sig rundt om, hvad den handling havde kostet ham. Bogen er kort — under 200 sider — og læses skiftevis som teologi, filosofisk drama, polemik mod Hegel og den omhyggeligt forklædte bekendelse fra en mand, der havde opgivet den kvinde, han elskede, uden at tro, at hun ville blive givet tilbage. Den er den kristne eksistentialismes grundtekst.

Dens virkning på senere tænkning har været vildt ude af proportion med dens længde. Heideggers læsning af angsten, Sartres beretning om springet, Bubers Jeg og Du, Levinas' etik om den absolut Anden, Derridas Dødens gave — alle vender tilbage til Frygt og Bæven. Det gør næsten enhver teologi fra det tyvende århundrede, der er villig til at tage troens forargelse alvorligt, også. Bogen nægter at gøre Abraham forståelig. Den insisterer på, at enhver udgave af religionen, der har gjort ham bekvem, er holdt op med at være religion. Argumentet har foruroliget både troende og ikke-troende i næsten to århundreder — og dukker stadig op, hver gang en offentlig person hævder at have modtaget privat guddommelig instruks.
after: Søren Kierkegaard udgav bogen i 1843 under navnet Johannes de silentio. Johannes vender tilbage til det øjeblik i Første Mosebog, hvor Abraham løfter kniven over Isak. Han begynder med fire forskellige måder at fortælle rejsen til Morija på. Ingen af dem gør Abraham lettere at forstå. Senere spørger han, hvordan man kan holde Abraham for troens far, når det etiske sprog kalder hans hensigt mord.

before.title: Den teleologiske suspension af det etiske.
before.text: Dette er bogens centrale påstand: Abrahams handling kan ikke retfærdiggøres af nogen universel morallov. Han er ikke Agamemnon, der ofrer Ifigenia for en offentlig sag. Han har ingen ydre grund at give Sara, ingen pligt at påberåbe sig, ingen tragedie at opføre. Troen, hævder Kierkegaard, sætter den enkelte i et direkte forhold til Gud, der står over det etiske — ikke ved at krænke det, men ved at suspendere det fra et højere udsigtspunkt. Læs med spørgsmålet, om et sådant udsigtspunkt overhovedet er muligt, eller om Kierkegaard blot har sat navn på en fare.
before.angleObjective: Jeg vil spore begrebet om den teleologiske suspension af det etiske gennem alle tre problemata — forstå, hvad Kierkegaard mener, hvorfor det ikke kan reduceres til nogen moralsk ramme, og hvad det indebærer for forholdet mellem religion og etik.

before.title: Troens ridder over for den uendelige resignations ridder.
before.text: Kierkegaard tegner en skarp kontrast mellem to svar på et umuligt tab. Den uendelige resignations ridder gør forsagelsens bevægelse fuldkomment — han opgiver Isak, accepterer tabet og finder en slags tragisk værdighed i sit offer. Men han får aldrig Isak tilbage. Troens ridder gør én bevægelse mere: han opgiver Isak og tror samtidig, i samme åndedrag, at han vil få ham tilbage. Kun den ene af de to skikkelser vender hjem. Læs med spørgsmålet, hvad den anden bevægelse faktisk kræver — og om du selv nogensinde har gjort den.
before.angleObjective: Jeg vil læse Frygt og Bæven for Kierkegaards sondring mellem uendelig resignation og tro — forstå, hvorfor resignation ikke er nok, hvad troens ekstra bevægelse består i, og om troens ridder er en skikkelse, noget menneske faktisk kan blive.

before.title: Mod Hegel: troen kan ikke medieres.
before.text: Bogen er en polemik. Dens mål er en kultur — personificeret i privatdocenter, spekulative filosoffer og selvtilfredse præster — der har slugt Hegel og nu tror, at troen blot er et tidligt trin af fornuften, en foreløbig bevægelse, som Systemet for længst har overskredet. Hele Kierkegaards anstrengelse går ud på at vise, at Abraham ikke hører hjemme i Systemet: han kan ikke forstås, medieres eller gøres bekvem. Den komiske parade af intellektuelle i forordet er allerede argumentet. Læs den som et angreb på idéen om, at filosofien har styr på troen.
before.angleObjective: Jeg vil læse Frygt og Bæven som en polemik mod den hegelianske kultur — følge, hvordan Kierkegaard bruger Abrahams tavshed og ufattelighed til at slå ethvert forsøg på rationel mediering tilbage, og spørge, hvad der står tilbage, når Systemets krav på troen er afvist.

before.title: Johannes de Silentio som forfejlet vidne.
before.text: Fortælleren er ikke Kierkegaard. Johannes de Silentio indrømmer åbent, fra første til sidste side, at han ikke er nogen troens ridder — at han ikke kan gøre bevægelsen, ikke kan forstå den, kun kan kredse og beundre og bekende sin egen uformåen. Det er ikke beskedenhed. Det er et strukturelt valg: bogen er skrevet udefra, fra et sted uden for troen, af en, der kan beskrive hver eneste kontur af det, han ikke kan eje. Læs med spørgsmålet, hvorfor Kierkegaard valgte denne stemme, og hvad det gør ved argumentet, at en filosof end ikke kan nærme sig dette emne i eget navn.
before.angleObjective: Jeg vil læse pseudonymet som et argument — spore, hvordan Johannes de Silentios indrømmede uformåen former hver eneste del af bogen, og spørge, hvad Kierkegaard opnår ved at nægte at tale i eget navn om noget, han ikke fuldt ud kan bebo.

after.title: Hør de fire fortællinger
after.text: Læg mærke til, hvem der mister noget i hver version af rejsen. Efter hver fortælling følger et billede af en mor, der vænner sit barn fra brystet. Hvad ændrer sig fra det ene billede til det næste?
after.angleObjective: Jeg vil læse de fire fortællinger hver for sig, før jeg sammenligner dem.

after.title: Følg den dobbelte bevægelse
after.text: Johannes kan forestille sig at give afkald på Isak. Hvad han ikke kan begribe, er, hvordan Abraham samtidig kan tro, at han får ham igen. Se efter, hvor forskellen viser sig i fortællingen om den unge mand og prinsessen.
after.angleObjective: Jeg vil forstå, hvad der adskiller den uendelige resignation fra troen.

after.title: Se, hvem der kan forklare sig
after.text: Agamemnon kan henvise til, at hele folkets skæbne er på spil. Isak er derimod Abrahams egen søn, og Abraham kan ikke pege på et fælles gode, som hans handling skal tjene.
after.angleObjective: Jeg vil sammenligne Abraham med de tragiske helte på det punkt, hvor de skal stå til ansvar.

after.title: Lyt til den, der taler
after.text: Johannes skifter mellem lovtale, spøg og argument. Han insisterer på, at han kan beundre Abraham uden selv at kunne handle som ham.
after.angleObjective: Jeg vil lægge mærke til, hvornår Johannes bekender noget om sig selv, og hvornår han stiller et spørgsmål til mig.

before.name: Abraham
before.description: Femoghalvfjerds år, da han først kaldes ud af Karan, hundrede, da Isak fødes, og gammel nok til at være hans oldefar, da han befales at bestige Morija. Han vandrer tre dage fra Beersheba i tavshed, bygger alteret, binder drengen, løfter kniven. Kierkegaard nægter at gøre ham til tragisk helt eller etisk forbillede. Abraham handler på en privat, absolut pligt, som han ikke kan oversætte til etikkens universelle sprog. Han er for Johannes de Silentio det største menneske, der nogensinde har levet — og det mest ufattelige.

before.name: Isaac
before.description: Forjættelsens barn, født af Sara som halvfemsårig og af Abraham som hundredårig. Gammel nok på vejen til Morija til selv at bære brændet til brændofferet og til at spørge sin fader, hvor lammet er. Kierkegaard forestiller sig fire forskellige udgaver af, hvad Isak ser på bjerget — heriblandt én, hvor Abraham med vilje får sig selv til at ligne en morder, for at Isak kan bevare sin tro på Gud. Fortællingen drejer sig om, hvorvidt Isak forstår, og om hvad der bevares mellem fader og søn, når de vandrer ned igen.

before.name: Johannes de Silentio
before.description: Kierkegaards maske. Skriver bogen fra en position af indrømmet uformåen. Han er ikke nogen troens ridder, kan ikke gøre bevægelsen og siger det på næsten hver side. Han kredser om Abraham med beundring, genfortæller historien på fire forskellige måder i Stemning og bekender igen og igen, at han ikke kan forstå, hvad Abraham gjorde. Utilstrækkeligheden er ikke retorisk ydmyghed. Den er Kierkegaards argument for, at troen ikke kan nærmes udefra, og at en filosof, der foregiver andet, bedrager sig selv.

before.name: The Knight of Faith
before.description: Kierkegaards højeste menneskelige type. Gør resignationens fulde bevægelse — opgiver den elskede, accepterer tabet absolut — og tror derpå, i kraft af det absurde, at han vil få det tilbage i dette liv. Abraham er det ypperste eksempel. Johannes beskriver en, der går ned ad Østergade i København og ligner en skatteopkræver på en prik, umulig at skelne fra spidsborgerne omkring ham, mens den uendelige bevægelse sker usynligt inde i ham. Fuldt hjemme i det endelige og fuldt vendt mod det uendelige i samme øjeblik.

before.name: The Knight of Infinite Resignation
before.description: Ædel, men utilstrækkelig. Har gjort forsagelsens bevægelse fuldkomment, opgivet det endelige til fordel for det uendelige og accepteret tabet uden klage. Lever i en slags tragisk værdighed, som den græske tragedie forstår og belønner. Men gør aldrig den videre bevægelse — tror aldrig, at den elskede vil blive givet tilbage. Han beholder tabet; troens ridder nægter at beholde det. Kierkegaard insisterer på, at resignationen er den letteste af de to, selvom den ser heroisk ud, fordi den bliver inden for kategorier, fornuften kan genkende.

before.name: Sarah
before.description: Abrahams hustru, Isaks moder, kvinden, der ventede halvfems år på et barn, og som ikke får at vide, hvad der sker, da hendes mand og hendes søn drager mod Morija ved daggry. Det tredje problema drejer sig om hende: Abraham kan ikke tale til Sara, fordi det, han gør, ikke lader sig oversætte til ægteskabets og familiens universelle sprog. Kierkegaard læser Abrahams tavshed over for hende som en del af det, der gør ham til troens ridder frem for tragisk helt. Sara er den omkostning, bogen stilfærdigt insisterer på.

after.name: Abraham
after.description: På vejen til Morija skal han både elske Isak og være rede til at ofre ham. Det er denne samtidighed, Johannes bliver ved med at vende tilbage til.

after.name: Isak
after.description: Han er sønnen, Abraham og Sara har ventet på. Hans spørgsmål om offerlammet fremkalder Abrahams eneste svar til ham på vejen.

after.name: Sara
after.description: I de fire fortællinger ser hun efter de rejsende, kysser sin søn eller løber ham i møde. I det tredje problem spørger Johannes, hvad Abraham skylder hende at fortælle.

after.name: Johannes de silentio
after.description: Han taler i eget navn. Han kan beskrive troens bevægelser og siger åbent, at han ikke selv kan foretage dem.

after.name: Agamemnon og Ifigenia
after.role: Den tragiske helt og hans datter
after.description: Agamemnons offer i Aulis giver Johannes et modstykke til Abraham. Datteren kan forstå, hvad en far, der handler for hele folket, mener at skylde det.

after.name: Troens ridder
after.description: Johannes forestiller sig en mand på søndagstur, der glæder sig til et stegt lammehoved. Hvad der foregår i hans tro, kan man ikke aflæse af hans gang eller appetit.

before.title: Hvad troen faktisk kræver
before.body: Bogen spørger, om troen er en trøst eller en forargelse. Kierkegaards svar er det sidste. Virkelig tro kræver, på hans regning, at den troende står alene foran Gud i det øjeblik, hvor hvert etisk princip, hvert socialt bånd, hver offentlig grund siger noget andet. Abraham kan ikke forklare sig over for Sara, over for Isak, over for det universelle. Han handler på en absolut pligt, der ikke lader sig oversætte. Argumentet har foruroliget kristen tænkning i næsten to århundreder. Det har gjort bekvemme former for religion sværere at forsvare, fordi Kierkegaards Abraham bliver ved med at dukke op og spørge, om de ville have gået op ad bjerget. Moderne læsere hører det, hver gang en offentlig person hævder at have modtaget privat guddommelig instruks, og et samfund må afgøre, om påstanden er ærefrygt, vrangforestilling eller noget værre.

before.title: Troens ridder
before.body: Kierkegaards billede af troens ridder er en af de mærkeligste skikkelser i den kristne tænknings historie. Han ser almindelig ud. Han er fuldt hjemme i det endelige — spiser sin middag, går ned ad gaden, umulig at skelne fra spidsborgerne omkring ham. Inde i ham foregår en uendelig bevægelse, som ingen ser. Han har opgivet alt og tror, at han vil få det tilbage. Billedet er den kristne eksistentialismes grundskikkelse. Det vender også romantikkens ideal om den synligt lidende helt på hovedet. Kierkegaard insisterer på, at virkelig tro ikke behøver at opføre sig selv som skuespil. Troens ridder er sværere at genkende end resignationens ridder, netop fordi intet ved ham røber hans tilstand. Hele inderligheden er pointen.

before.title: Det universelles grænser
before.body: Kierkegaard hævder, at der findes øjeblikke, hvor den enkeltes forhold til Gud står højere end den universelle morallov. Han kalder det den teleologiske suspension af det etiske. Han ved også, at argumentet er farligt. Den foreløbige expectoration bruger side efter side på at skelne Abraham fra en fanatiker, og problemata insisterer på, at suspensionen ikke kan påberåbes som fribrev, fordi troens ridder ikke kan give nogen offentlig redegørelse for, hvorfor han er undtaget fra det universelle — det er netop hans vilkår. Bogen lader faren stå urørt. De spørgsmål, den rejser om autoritet, samvittighed og etikkens grænser, står stadig åbne. Hver gang nogen hævder at have hørt fra Gud imod den moralske konsensus, er Kierkegaards diagnostiske kategorier stadig de skarpeste, der findes.

after.title: Prøv fortællingen på dens sværeste sted
after.body: Det er let at sige, at Abraham gav Gud det bedste, han havde. Johannes beder os sætte navnet Isak tilbage i sætningen. Så får også en fars pligt over for sit barn en stemme.

after.title: Tag tavsheden alvorligt
after.body: Brudgommen i Delfi, Agnete og havmanden og tvivleren Faust viser vidt forskellige grunde til at tie. Med dem som baggrund bliver det mere præcist, hvad Johannes mener, når han siger, at Abraham ikke kan tale.

after.title: Læs uden at kende udfaldet på forhånd
after.body: Vi ved, at vædderen står på bjerget. Abraham har endnu hverken set den eller hævet kniven. Den forskel beder Johannes os blive ved længe nok til at mærke.

before: Preface + Exordium + Eulogy + Preliminary Expectoration + 3 Problemata + Epilogue (8 chapters)
after: A preface, four variations on Abraham, a eulogy, a preliminary outpouring, three philosophical problems, and an epilogue

before: Not just in the world of commerce but also in the world of ideas, our age has set up a real auction. Everything can be had so cheap that it becomes a question whether anyone will end up wanting to bid. Every speculative philosopher who conscientiously marks out the significant march of modern thought, every lecturer, tutor, and student — not one stops at doubting everything. They go further. Perhaps it would be untimely and impolite to ask where exactly they are going, but it is surely polite and modest to assume they have already doubted everything, since otherwise it would be a strange way to speak — going further.
after:
A dialectical lyric by Johannes de silentio.

_Was Tarquinius Superbus in seinem Garten mit den Mohnköpfen sprach, verstand der Sohn, aber nicht der Bote._ — Hamann
[The son understood what Tarquinius Superbus said with the poppy heads in his garden, but the messenger did not.]

Our age is putting on ein wirklicher Ausverkauf — a genuine clearance sale — and not only in trade: in the realm of ideas too. Everything can be had at such a rock-bottom price that one begins to wonder whether in the end anyone will still want to bid. Every speculative billiard-marker who conscientiously keeps score of the momentous progress of modern philosophy, every private lecturer, tutor and student, every smallholder and lodger in philosophy, does not stop at doubting everything but goes further. It would perhaps be untimely and inopportune to ask them where they actually get to. But it is surely polite and modest to take it as settled that they have doubted everything; otherwise it would be a strange thing to say, that they went further. This preliminary movement, then, they have all made — and presumably so easily that they do not find it necessary to let fall a single word about how. For not even the person who anxiously and with concern looked for a little enlightenment found any: not a guiding hint, not a small dietary prescription for how one is to conduct oneself under this enormous task. “But surely Descartes did it?” Descartes, a venerable, humble and upright thinker whose writings no one, surely, can read without the deepest emotion, did as he said and said as he did. Alas! Alas! Alas! In our time that is a great rarity! Descartes, as he himself repeats often enough, did not doubt with regard to faith. (“Memores tamen, ut jam dictum est, huic lumini naturali tamdiu tantum esse credendum, quamdiu nihil contrarium a Deo ipso revelatur ..... Præter cætera autem, memoriæ nostræ pro summa regula est infigendum, ea quæ nobis a Deo revelata sunt, ut omnium certissima esse credenda; et quamvis forte lumen rationis, quam maxime clarum et evidens, aliud quid nobis suggerere videretur, soli tamen auctoritati divinæ potius quam proprio nostro judicio fidem esse adhibendam.” [Remembering, however, as has already been said, that this natural light is to be trusted only so long as nothing to the contrary is revealed by God himself ..... Above all, though, we must fix in our memory as the supreme rule that what God has revealed to us is to be believed as the most certain of all things; and even if perhaps the light of reason, however clear and evident, should seem to suggest something else to us, we must still put our faith in divine authority alone rather than in our own judgment.] Cf. Principia philosophiæ, part one, § 28 and § 76.) He did not cry “Fire!” and make it everyone’s duty to doubt; for Descartes was a quiet, solitary thinker, not a bellowing night watchman in the street. He modestly admitted that his method had significance only for himself, and that it arose in part from the muddle his earlier learning had been in. (“Ne quis igitur putet, me hic traditurum aliquam methodum, quam unusquisque sequi debeat ad recte regendam rationem; illam enim tantum, quam ipsemet secutus sum, exponere decrevi... Sed simul ac illud studiorum curriculum absolvi (sc. juventutis, quo decurso mos est in eruditorum numerum cooptari, plane aliud coepi cogitare. Tot enim me dubiis totque erroribus implicatum esse animadverti, ut omnes discendi conatus nihil aliud mihi profuisse judicarem, quam quod ignorantiam meam magis magisque detexissem.” [So let no one suppose that I mean to hand down here some method that everyone ought to follow in order to guide his reason rightly; for I have resolved to set out only the one I myself have followed... But as soon as I had finished that course of study (namely, of my youth), at the end of which it is the custom to be admitted to the ranks of the learned, I began to think something quite different. For I found myself entangled in so many doubts and so many errors that I judged that all my efforts to learn had done me no other good than to uncover my ignorance more and more.] Cf. Dissertatio de methodo, pp. 2 and 3.) — The ancient Greeks, who did after all know something about philosophy too, held doubting to be the task of a whole life, because the skill of doubting is not acquired in days or weeks. The old veteran among them, who had served his full time, attained it: through every snare he had held doubt in equilibrium, had fearlessly denied the certainty of the senses and the certainty of thought, and had incorruptibly withstood the anxiety of self-love and the insinuations of fellow-feeling. What the Greeks took for a life’s task and their veteran attained — that is what everyone in our time begins with.

before:
Fear and Trembling circles a single story from Genesis 22: God commands Abraham to take his son Isaac up Mount Moriah and kill him as a burnt offering, and Abraham obeys. He saddles his ass at dawn, walks three days in silence, builds the altar, binds his son, and raises the knife. The angel stays his hand. The book asks how it is possible to call this man the father of faith rather than a murderer, and what kind of faith would be required to be him. Kierkegaard rewrites the Moriah story four different ways in the opening pages. He compares Abraham with Agamemnon at Aulis, with the tragic hero of Greek drama, with Mary at the annunciation, with the merman of Danish folktale. Around the story he builds a systematic argument about three Problemata: whether there is a teleological suspension of the ethical, whether there is an absolute duty to God, whether Abraham's silence to Sarah and Isaac was ethically defensible.

Kierkegaard published it in Copenhagen in October 1843, at thirty, under the pseudonym Johannes de Silentio, the same week he published Repetition. He had broken his engagement to Regine Olsen two years earlier and could not stop writing his way around what that act had cost him. The book is short — under 200 pages — and reads in turns as theology, philosophical drama, polemic against Hegel, and the elaborately disguised confession of a man who had given up the woman he loved without believing she would be returned to him. It is the founding text of Christian existentialism.

Its effect on later thought has been wildly disproportionate to its length. Heidegger's reading of anxiety, Sartre's account of the leap, Buber's I and Thou, Levinas's ethics of the absolute Other, Derrida's Gift of Death — all return to Fear and Trembling. So does almost every twentieth-century theology willing to take the offence of faith seriously. The book refuses to make Abraham comprehensible. It insists that any version of religion that has made him comfortable has stopped being religion. The argument has unsettled both the believing and the unbelieving for nearly two centuries — and continues to surface whenever a public figure claims private divine instruction.
after: Søren Kierkegaard published this book in 1843 as Johannes de silentio. Johannes keeps returning to the moment in Genesis when Abraham raises the knife over Isaac. He begins with four different ways of telling the journey to Moriah. None makes Abraham easier to understand. Later he asks how Abraham can be called the father of faith when the ethical description of what he intends to do is murder.

before.title: The teleological suspension of the ethical.
before.text: This is the book's central claim: Abraham's act cannot be justified by any universal moral law. He is not Agamemnon sacrificing Iphigenia for a public cause. He has no external reason to give Sarah, no duty to invoke, no tragedy to perform. Faith, Kierkegaard argues, places the individual in a direct relationship with God that stands above the ethical — not by violating it, but by suspending it from a higher vantage point. Read asking whether any such vantage point is possible, or whether Kierkegaard has simply named a danger.
before.angleObjective: I want to trace the concept of the teleological suspension of the ethical through all three Problemata — understanding what Kierkegaard means, why it cannot be reduced to any moral framework, and what this implies for the relationship between religion and ethics.

before.title: Knight of faith vs. knight of infinite resignation.
before.text: Kierkegaard draws a stark contrast between two responses to an impossible loss. The knight of infinite resignation makes the movement of renunciation perfectly — he gives up Isaac, accepts the loss, and finds a kind of tragic dignity in his sacrifice. But he never gets Isaac back. The knight of faith makes one further movement: he gives up Isaac and simultaneously, in the same breath, believes he will receive him back. Only one of these figures returns home. Read asking what the second movement actually requires — and whether you have ever made it.
before.angleObjective: I want to read Fear and Trembling for Kierkegaard's distinction between infinite resignation and faith — understanding why resignation is not enough, what the additional movement of faith consists in, and whether the knight of faith is a figure anyone can actually become.

before.title: Against Hegel: faith cannot be mediated.
before.text: The book is a polemic. Its target is a culture — personified in assistant professors, speculative philosophers, and smug clergymen — that has swallowed Hegel and now believes faith is merely an early stage of reason, a preliminary movement that the System has long since surpassed. Kierkegaard's entire effort is to show that Abraham does not belong in the System: he cannot be understood, mediated, or made comfortable. The comic parade of intellectuals in the Preface is already the argument. Read it as an attack on the idea that philosophy has faith covered.
before.angleObjective: I want to read Fear and Trembling as a polemic against Hegelian culture — tracking how Kierkegaard uses Abraham's silence and unintelligibility to defeat every attempt at rational mediation, and asking what survives once the System's claim over faith is rejected.

before.title: Johannes de Silentio as a failed witness.
before.text: The narrator is not Kierkegaard. Johannes de Silentio openly admits, from the first page to the last, that he is not a knight of faith — that he cannot make the movement, cannot understand it, can only circle and admire and confess his own incapacity. This is not modesty. It is a structural choice: the book is written from outside faith, by someone who can describe every contour of what he cannot possess. Read asking why Kierkegaard chose this voice, and what it does to the argument that a philosopher cannot even approach this topic in his own name.
before.angleObjective: I want to read the pseudonym as an argument — tracing how Johannes de Silentio's admitted incapacity shapes every section of the book, and asking what Kierkegaard accomplishes by refusing to speak in his own name about something he cannot fully inhabit.

after.title: Listen to the four tellings
after.text: Notice who loses something in each version of the journey. Each is followed by an image of a mother weaning her child. What changes from one image to the next?
after.angleObjective: I want to read each telling on its own before comparing them.

after.title: Follow the double movement
after.text: Johannes can imagine giving Isaac up. What he cannot grasp is how Abraham can also believe that he will get Isaac back. Look for the distinction in the story of the young man and the princess.
after.angleObjective: I want to understand the difference between infinite resignation and faith.

after.title: Ask who can explain himself
after.text: Agamemnon can point to the fate of a whole people. Isaac is Abraham’s own son, and Abraham can name no common good that his act would serve.
after.angleObjective: I want to compare Abraham with the tragic heroes at the moment they must answer for what they do.

after.title: Listen to the speaker
after.text: Johannes moves between praise, jokes, and argument. He insists that he can admire Abraham without being able to act as Abraham did.
after.angleObjective: I want to notice when Johannes admits something about himself and when he puts a question to me.

before.name: Abraham
before.description: Seventy-five when first called out of Haran, a hundred when Isaac is born, and old enough to be his great-grandfather when commanded to climb Moriah. Walks three days from Beersheba in silence, builds the altar, binds the boy, raises the knife. Kierkegaard refuses to make him a tragic hero or an ethical exemplar. Abraham acts on a private absolute duty he cannot translate into the universal language of ethics. He is, for Johannes de Silentio, the greatest human being who ever lived — and the most incomprehensible.

before.name: Isaac
before.description: The child of promise, born to Sarah at ninety and to Abraham at a hundred. Old enough on the road to Moriah to carry the wood for the burnt offering himself, and to ask his father where the lamb is. Kierkegaard imagines four different versions of what Isaac sees on the mountain — including one in which Abraham deliberately makes himself look like a murderer so that Isaac can keep his faith in God. The story turns on whether Isaac understands and on what is preserved between father and son when they walk back down.

before.name: Johannes de Silentio
before.description: Kierkegaard's mask. Writes the book from a position of admitted incapacity. He is not a knight of faith, cannot make the movement, and says so on almost every page. He circles Abraham with admiration, rewrites the story four different ways in the Exordium, and confesses again and again that he cannot understand what Abraham did. The inadequacy is not rhetorical humility. It is Kierkegaard's argument that faith cannot be approached from outside, and that a philosopher who pretends otherwise is deceiving himself.

before.name: The Knight of Faith
before.description: Kierkegaard's highest human type. Makes the full movement of resignation — giving up the beloved, accepting the loss absolutely — and then, by virtue of the absurd, believes he will receive it back in this life. Abraham is the supreme instance. Johannes describes one walking down Østergade in Copenhagen looking exactly like a tax-collector, indistinguishable from the burghers around him, the infinite movement happening invisibly inside him. Fully at home in the finite and fully oriented toward the infinite at the same instant.

before.name: The Knight of Infinite Resignation
before.description: Noble but insufficient. Has made the movement of renunciation perfectly, surrendered the finite in favor of the infinite, and accepted loss without complaint. Lives with a kind of tragic dignity that Greek tragedy understands and rewards. But never makes the further movement — never believes the beloved will be returned. He keeps the loss; the knight of faith refuses to. Kierkegaard insists resignation is the easier of the two, even though it looks heroic, because it stays within categories reason can recognize.

before.name: Sarah
before.role: The Wife on the Other Side
before.description: Abraham's wife, Isaac's mother, the woman who waited ninety years for a child and who is not told what is happening when her husband and her son leave for Moriah at dawn. The third Problema turns on her: Abraham cannot speak to Sarah because what he is doing admits no translation into the universal language of marriage and family. Kierkegaard reads Abraham's silence to her as part of what makes him a knight of faith rather than a tragic hero. Sarah is the cost the book quietly insists on.

after.name: Abraham
after.description: On the road to Moriah he must love Isaac and be ready to offer him up. It is the coexistence of those two things that keeps drawing Johannes back.

after.name: Isaac
after.description: He is the son for whom Abraham and Sarah have waited. His question about the lamb draws Abraham’s one recorded reply to him on the journey.

after.name: Sarah
after.description: Across the four tellings, she watches the travelers depart, kisses her son, or runs out to meet them. The third problem asks what Abraham owes it to her to say.

after.name: Johannes de silentio
after.description: He speaks in his own name. He can describe the movements of faith and freely admits that he cannot make them himself.

after.name: Agamemnon and Iphigenia
after.role: A tragic hero and his daughter
after.description: The sacrifice at Aulis provides a contrast with Abraham. A daughter can understand what a father believes he owes to the whole people.

after.name: The knight of faith
after.description: Johannes pictures a man on a Sunday outing looking forward to a roasted lamb’s head. Neither his gait nor his appetite gives his faith away.

before.title: What Faith Actually Requires
before.body: The book asks whether faith is a comfort or a scandal. Kierkegaard's answer is the second. Real faith, on his account, asks the believer to stand alone before God in the moment when every ethical principle, every social bond, every public reason says otherwise. Abraham cannot explain himself to Sarah, to Isaac, to the universal. He acts on an absolute duty that admits no translation. The argument has unsettled Christian thought for nearly two centuries. It has made comfortable forms of religion harder to defend, because Kierkegaard's Abraham keeps showing up to ask whether they would have made the climb. Modern readers hear it whenever a public figure claims private divine instruction and a society has to decide whether the claim is reverence, delusion, or worse.

before.title: The Knight of Faith
before.body: Kierkegaard's image of the knight of faith is one of the strangest figures in the history of Christian thought. He looks ordinary. He is fully at home in the finite — eats his dinner, walks down the street, indistinguishable from the burghers around him. Inside him an infinite movement is happening that no one sees. He has given up everything and believes he will get it back. The image is the founding figure of Christian existentialism. It also reverses the Romantic ideal of the visibly suffering hero. Kierkegaard insists that real faith does not need to perform itself. The knight of faith is harder to recognize than the knight of resignation precisely because nothing about him announces his condition. The whole inwardness is the point.

before.title: The Limits of the Universal
before.body: Kierkegaard argues that there are moments when the individual's relationship to God is higher than the universal moral law. He calls this the teleological suspension of the ethical. He also knows the argument is dangerous. The Preliminary Expectoration spends pages distinguishing Abraham from a fanatic, and the Problemata insist that the suspension cannot be claimed as a license, because the knight of faith can give no public account of why he is exempt from the universal — that is exactly his condition. The book leaves the danger intact. The questions it raises about authority, conscience, and the limits of ethics remain open. Whenever someone claims to have heard from God against the moral consensus, Kierkegaard's diagnostic categories are still the sharpest available.

after.title: Put the son back into the story
after.body: It is easy to say that Abraham gave God the best he had. Johannes asks us to put Isaac’s name back in that sentence. A father’s duty to his child then makes a claim of its own.

after.title: Take silence seriously
after.body: The bridegroom of Delphi, Agnes and the merman, and Faust the doubter have very different reasons for keeping silent. Their stories sharpen the question of what Johannes means when he says that Abraham cannot speak.

after.title: Read before the outcome is known
after.body: We know that the ram is on the mountain. Abraham has neither seen it nor raised the knife yet. Johannes asks us to stay with that difference long enough to feel it.
